topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Eyes
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: The Hook: The Map Dilemma
sections.content: Introduce the concept that the 'coordinates' of a point depend entirely on the 'map' (basis) you are using. Use a narrative approach to show that the same physical location can have different numerical labels.
sections.example: Two explorers, Alice and Bob, are in a desert. Alice uses a standard North-East grid. Bob uses a grid aligned with a slanted canyon and a distant oasis. They are looking at the same treasure chest. Alice says it's at (3, 4), but Bob needs to know what that means in his 'slanted' coordinate system.

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
sections.content: Quickly review that a basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that span a space. Visually represent the Standard Basis (i, j) as a rigid square grid.
sections.example: Show a 2D plane with unit vectors e1 (1,0) and e2 (0,1). Demonstrate how any vector 'v' is just a recipe: 3 steps of e1 and 2 steps of e2.

sections.title: The New Perspective: Non-Standard Basis
sections.content: Introduce a new basis 'B' consisting of two vectors, b1 and b2, that are not at right angles. Graphically overlay a 'skewed' or 'tilted' grid on top of the standard grid to show how space is re-measured.
sections.example: Visual: A robot is programmed to move along a basis B where b1 = (2, 1) and b2 = (-1, 1). Show the robot's world-view as a diamond-shaped grid instead of a square one.

sections.title: The Bridge: The Change of Basis Matrix
sections.content: Explain the 'Transition Matrix' (P). This matrix acts as a translator. Key concept: The columns of the transition matrix from B to the standard basis are simply the coordinates of b1 and b2 written in the standard basis.
sections.example: To translate Bob's coordinates back to Alice's, we build a matrix P where Column 1 is Bob's first vector (2, 1) and Column 2 is Bob's second vector (-1, 1). Animation shows the standard grid morphing/stretching into Bob's grid.

sections.title: The Mathematical Transformation
sections.content: Present the core formula: [v]standard = P * [v]B and [v]B = P⁻¹ * [v]standard. Emphasize that P inverse is the 'decoder' that takes us from the standard world into the custom basis world.
sections.example: Calculation: If a point is at (1, 1) in Bob's slanted system, what is it for Alice? We multiply the matrix P by the vector [1, 1] to get the result (1, 2) in Alice's standard system.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
sections.content: Show how change of basis is used in gaming or CGI to calculate how a character 'sees' an object compared to how the 'world' sees it (Camera Space vs. World Space).
sections.example: A flying dragon (the character) has its own forward/up/side basis. As it tilts its wings, its internal basis changes. To render the sun in the dragon's eyes, the computer performs a Change of Basis from 'World Coordinates' to 'Dragon Coordinates'.

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
sections.content: Wrap up by reinforcing that a vector is an absolute 'arrow' in space; only its 'name' (coordinates) changes when we change our perspective (basis).
sections.example: Animation: The treasure chest stays in the same spot while the grid lines under it spin and stretch, showing the coordinates changing from (3,4) to (1.5, 2.2) while the physical location remains fixed.
